screens.title: What is Static Analysis?
screens.narratorSegment: Static analysis is the automated inspection of source code without running the program. That means tools parse and reason about the program structure, types, and usage to identify patterns that commonly lead to bugs: uninitialized variables, unsafe pointer usage, unnecessary copies, or non-modern idioms. A clear example is catching an uninitialized local variable: a static checker can reason that a code path returns a value that was never assigned. Static analysis complements, but does not replace, testing. Tests exercise behavior at runtime and find logical errors that depend on inputs, while static tools find issues that are visible from the code shape itself. A common misconception is that static analysis finds every bug; it cannot detect runtime-only behavior like environment-dependent logic or race conditions—those need sanitizers or dynamic testing. Another misconception is to treat every warning as an error immediately; on a legacy codebase, enable checks selectively and escalate gradually. Takeaway: static analysis reduces the feedback loop for many classes of defects, saving time during debugging and code review. Ask yourself: which kinds of bugs in your project would be cheaper to catch before the first test run?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › What is Static Analysis?
Core Concept

Static analysis defined

Tools inspect source without executing it, reasoning about control flow, types, and usage to detect likely problems before running code.

Why it matters
  • Catches errors early, reducing time spent debugging runtime failures.
  • Enforces best practices and helps modernize legacy code.
  • Reduces reviewer effort by surfacing obvious issues automatically.
Concrete example
A checker flags an uninitialized variable before execution. This prevents undefined output and a hard-to-reproduce crash at runtime.
Common mistake
Expecting static analysis to catch runtime-only errors like data races; use sanitizers and tests for those.
Key Takeaway

Static analysis is a fast, pre-execution safety net that finds many bug classes and improves maintainability.

Analogy

Think of static analysis as an editor that flags suspicious patterns the moment code is written, while tests are like running the program to confirm behavior under inputs.

Checklist to adopt static analysis
  1. Choose a primary tool (Clang-Tidy recommended for C++).
  2. Generate compile_commands.json so checks run with correct flags.
  3. Start with a limited set of checks and expand gradually.
Quick code snippet (illustrative)
// Example: problematic use of uninitialized variable
int compute() {
  int x; // uninitialized
  if (some_condition()) {
    x = 5;
  }
  return x; // static analysis can warn here
}

screens.title: Static Analysis vs Runtime Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Static analysis and runtime sanitizers serve different but complementary roles. Static checks inspect code shape and logic without execution, catching issues like uninitialized variables, non-modern idioms, and likely null dereferences. Runtime sanitizers, such as the AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, instrument and run the program to detect memory errors and undefined behavior that only appear during execution. For example, a use-after-free might not be visible statically in complex code, but AddressSanitizer will report it at runtime with a stack trace. A common mistake is relying solely on static analysis and assuming all memory problems will be found; conversely, relying only on sanitizers misses patterns that are easy to spot without running code. Use both: static analysis to reduce the number of obvious code-style and likely-bug issues, and sanitizers during testing to catch memory and concurrency problems. Integrate static checks in pre-commit or CI, and run sanitizers during dedicated test runs with debug symbols. Closing question: which scenarios in your codebase are more likely to be found statically, and which require runtime instrumentation? Static Analysis vs Runtime Tools means static analysis finds structural issues early; sanitizers catch memory and runtime errors during execution.. In practical terms, how clang-tidy and sanitizers complement each other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Static vs Runtime
Comparison

Static tools (Clang-Tidy)

Analyze code without running it to find uninitialized variables, modernize suggestions, and style or bug-prone patterns.

Strengths
  • Fast, runs on source only
  • Integrates with CI and editors
  • Detects many common mistakes before runtime
Limitations
Cannot reliably detect race conditions or some dynamic memory errors that only appear when code executes with certain inputs.
Comparison

Runtime tools (Sanitizers)

Instrument code at compile and runtime to detect memory errors, undefined behavior, and threading issues when tests execute.

Strengths
  • Pinpoints actual runtime errors with stack traces
  • Effective for memory bugs like use-after-free
  • Works well in dedicated test runs
Limitations
Slower test runs and environment-dependent failures; not a replacement for static checks that find issues early.
Concrete scenario

A code path with conditional freeing may evade static detection but trigger AddressSanitizer; combine both tools for broad coverage.

screens.title: Clang-Tidy: Checks and Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Clang-Tidy organizes diagnostics into named checks with a category prefix, for example modernize-use-nullptr or bugprone-uninitialized-local-variable. A typical configuration lives in a. clang-tidy YAML file at the project root where you list Checks and other options. A common pattern is to enable broad categories with a wildcard and then explicitly disable specific checks you don’t want. For instance, Checks: 'clang-diagnostic-*,modernize-*,readability-*,bugprone-*,-readability-magic-numbers' enables many useful rules but excludes magic-number noise. The compilation database is essential because Clang-Tidy uses the exact compiler flags and include paths from compile_commands. json to parse each file correctly. A frequent misconception is that more checks are always better; on a large legacy codebase, enabling everything creates too many warnings. Instead, start with a curated set, run fixes iteratively, and expand checks as the code stabilizes. Integrate Clang-Tidy into CI and treat new warnings as gating criteria. Which checks would you enable first to reduce high-confidence defects in your code? Clang-Tidy: Checks and Configuration means use .clang-tidy to enable categories and selectively disable rules; start small and grow the checks list over time.. In practical terms, how checks are named and how to enable or disable them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Clang-Tidy
Tool Overview

Clang-Tidy checks

Checks are named by category, and .clang-tidy controls which run. Enable broad groups then fine-tune per project.

# .clang-tidy example
Checks: 'clang-diagnostic-*,modernize-*,readability-*,bugprone-*,-readability-magic-numbers'
WarningsAsErrors: ''
FormatStyle: file
Best practice
Start with a conservative set of checks and treat new warnings as the codebase improves; avoid enabling everything at once.
Misconception
Disabling a check is acceptable if the rule conflicts with project constraints, but document why you disabled it.
Key Takeaway

Tune checks deliberately: enable high-value rules first, then expand as the team addresses warnings.

How checks look
Example checks
  • modernize-use-nullptr — prefer nullptr over NULL or 0
  • bugprone-uninitialized-local-variable — warn when a variable may be used uninitialized
  • readability-else-after-return — simplify branches after a return
Compilation database
Generate compile_commands.json with CMake by setting CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS to ON so Clang-Tidy parses files with correct flags.

screens.title: Generate compile_commands.json with CMake
screens.narratorSegment: Clang-Tidy needs to know how each file is compiled. The standard way to supply this information is a compilation database named compile_commands. json. With CMake you enable this by setting CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS to ON, then configuring the project. Practically, create a build directory, run cmake.. from that directory, and CMake will write compile_commands. json into the build tree. A common workflow is: create the source tree with CMakeLists. txt, set the export option, run cmake from a clean build folder, and then run clang-tidy with -p pointing to that build folder. A misconception is expecting compile_commands. json in the source root automatically; it lives in the build directory that CMake produced. Another subtlety: some build systems or wrapper tools move or rewrite paths, so verify the paths in compile_commands. json match your source layout. Key takeaway: always generate the compilation database before running Clang-Tidy so diagnostics reflect actual compiler flags and include paths. Generate compile_commands.json with CMake means it provides per-file compile flags and include paths so static checks parse files accurately.. In practical terms, provide context so clang-tidy analyzes files with real flags and includes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Generate compile_commands.json
Process Flow

Create the compilation database

Follow these steps to produce compile_commands.json so Clang-Tidy runs with full context.

1. Add to CMakeLists
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)
2. Create build dir
mkdir build && cd build
3. Run CMake
cmake ..
Run Clang-Tidy with the DB
clang-tidy -p build_directory/path/to/source_file.cpp
# Or use a wrapper to run across the whole database
python /path/to/run-clang-tidy.py -p build_directory
Tip
Confirm paths inside compile_commands.json if Clang-Tidy shows missing headers.
Pitfall
Don't expect compile_commands.json in the source root; look in the build folder created by CMake.
Key Takeaway

Generate and point Clang-Tidy to the compilation database so diagnostics reflect real compile flags.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Sample Project
Code Walkthrough

CMakeLists.txt

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.10)
project(MyQualityProject CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

# Generate compilation database for Clang-Tidy
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

add_executable(my_app src/main.cpp)
Code Walkthrough

src/main.cpp (problematic)

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int calculate_discount(int price) {
    if(price > 100) {
        return price - (price * 10 / 100);
    }
    return price;
}

void process_data() {
    int uninitialized_value;
    std::cout << "Uninitialized value: " << uninitialized_value << std::endl;

    std::vector data;
    data.push_back(1);
    data.push_back(2);
    for(int i = 0; i < data.size(); i++) {
        std::cout << data[i] << " ";
    }
    std::cout << std::endl;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << "Hello, Quality World!" << std::endl;
    int final_price = calculate_discount(150);
    std::cout << "Discounted price: " << final_price << std::endl;
    process_data();
    return 0;
}
Run this sequence
mkdir build && cd build cmake .. clang-format -i ../src/main.cpp clang-tidy -p . ../src/main.cpp
Expected results
  • main.cpp is reformatted according to .clang-format
  • Clang-Tidy warns about the uninitialized variable and suggests modernizing the loop
Key Takeaway

Use a small project to iterate: format first, then run static checks with a compilation database for accurate diagnostics.

screens.title: Understanding Clang-Tidy Warnings
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting Clang-Tidy output is a key skill. Warnings typically include a diagnostic name that hints at the problem and a short message with a source location. Two instructive examples from the sample main. cpp are an uninitialized local variable and a loop modernization suggestion. The uninitialized-local-variable warning indicates code paths where a variable may be used before assignment; this often points to missing initialization or a control-flow gap. The modernize-loop-convert suggestion recommends replacing an old-style index loop over a container with a range-based for loop to improve readability and reduce off-by-one risks. A misconception is to blindly apply every automated fix: modernize transformations are often safe but can change performance characteristics or semantics in edge cases. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Interpreting Warnings
Example

bugprone-uninitialized-local-variable

This diagnostic points to a variable that may be used without initialization. The remedy is to initialize the variable or adjust control flow.

int uninitialized_value;
std::cout << uninitialized_value; // warning: uninitialized local variable
Example

modernize-loop-convert

Suggests using a range-based for loop instead of indexing the container manually for clarity and safety.

for(int i = 0; i < data.size(); i++) {
  std::cout << data[i] << " ";
}
// Suggested: for (int v : data) { std::cout << v << " "; }
Fix and re-run
After applying a change, run clang-tidy again to ensure the diagnostic is resolved and no new ones appear.
Caution
Automated fixes can sometimes alter behavior; always review fixes before committing.

Read the diagnostic name and message, apply a careful fix, and re-run checks to confirm the issue is gone.

screens.title: Other Tools and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond Clang-Tidy and Clang-Format, the C++ ecosystem includes tools that cover different needs. Cppcheck provides fast, focused static checks and can be a lightweight complement. Commercial options like PVS-Studio and Coverity provide deeper, enterprise-grade diagnostics for complex codebases. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we’ll make static analysis and automated formatting approachable and practical. You will learn why analyzing code without running it catches many bugs earlier, and how automated formatting keeps teams consistent so reviewers focus on logic, not style. We’ll use two LLVM tools: Clang-Tidy for checks that find bugs, unsafe patterns, and modernization opportunities, and Clang-Format for applying a single, project-wide style automatically. Along the way you’ll see how to generate the compilation database that these tools need, how to author. clang-tidy and. clang-format files, and how to add checks incrementally so you don’t overwhelm a large codebase. You’ll also meet complementary options like Cppcheck and sanitizers for runtime detection. By the end you’ll have a repeatable approach: generate your compile_commands. json, pick a conservative Clang-Tidy configuration, run formatting automatically, and integrate these steps into build and CI. Think of this as building a safety net for your repository: it finds likely mistakes early, reduces review noise, and protects your team from regressions. Ready to explore how to configure and run these tools on a small project?

These objectives map to concrete capabilities you can apply in real C++ projects. First, you will be able to explain what static analysis is and why analyzing code without running it finds certain classes of bugs earlier than runtime tests. For example, Clang-Tidy can flag an uninitialized local variable before you reproduce a crash. Second, you will learn to generate and use a compilation database and to run Clang-Tidy with project context so warnings are accurate for each translation unit. Third, you will configure Clang-Format with a team style and use its in-place formatting to remove style debates from code review. Finally, you will learn how to automate these steps—format on save, pre-commit hooks, and CI integration—so your team gets consistent enforcement. Each objective emphasizes practical steps and why they matter: fewer runtime regressions, clearer reviews, and a maintainable codebase. As you progress, test each objective by running the provided hands-on workflow and observing how warnings and formatting change.

This second objectives slide focuses on measurable outcomes you can try immediately. You will create a small CMake project and enable export of compile_commands. json so Clang-Tidy sees exact compiler options. You will author. clang-tidy and. clang-format examples and run clang-format -i to reformat files and clang-tidy -p to analyze them. The hands-on walkthrough in this chapter guides you through creating the sample project, running formatting, and inspecting Clang-Tidy warnings such as uninitialized local variables and suggestions to modernize loops. You will practice toggling a check like readability-magic-numbers to see how configuration changes the output. Finally, you will learn when to treat warnings as errors in CI and when to disable a rule because project constraints make it inappropriate. Verifying competency means you can run the provided commands, interpret at least two warnings, and demonstrate consistent formatting across the sample files.

Static analysis is the automated inspection of source code without running the program. That means tools parse and reason about the program structure, types, and usage to identify patterns that commonly lead to bugs: uninitialized variables, unsafe pointer usage, unnecessary copies, or non-modern idioms. A clear example is catching an uninitialized local variable: a static checker can reason that a code path returns a value that was never assigned. Static analysis complements, but does not replace, testing. Tests exercise behavior at runtime and find logical errors that depend on inputs, while static tools find issues that are visible from the code shape itself. A common misconception is that static analysis finds every bug; it cannot detect runtime-only behavior like environment-dependent logic or race conditions—those need sanitizers or dynamic testing. Another misconception is to treat every warning as an error immediately; on a legacy codebase, enable checks selectively and escalate gradually. Takeaway: static analysis reduces the feedback loop for many classes of defects, saving time during debugging and code review. Ask yourself: which kinds of bugs in your project would be cheaper to catch before the first test run?

Static analysis and runtime sanitizers serve different but complementary roles. Static checks inspect code shape and logic without execution, catching issues like uninitialized variables, non-modern idioms, and likely null dereferences. Runtime sanitizers, such as the AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, instrument and run the program to detect memory errors and undefined behavior that only appear during execution. For example, a use-after-free might not be visible statically in complex code, but AddressSanitizer will report it at runtime with a stack trace. A common mistake is relying solely on static analysis and assuming all memory problems will be found; conversely, relying only on sanitizers misses patterns that are easy to spot without running code. Use both: static analysis to reduce the number of obvious code-style and likely-bug issues, and sanitizers during testing to catch memory and concurrency problems. Integrate static checks in pre-commit or CI, and run sanitizers during dedicated test runs with debug symbols. Closing question: which scenarios in your codebase are more likely to be found statically, and which require runtime instrumentation? Static Analysis vs Runtime Tools means static analysis finds structural issues early; sanitizers catch memory and runtime errors during execution.. In practical terms, how clang-tidy and sanitizers complement each other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Clang-Tidy organizes diagnostics into named checks with a category prefix, for example modernize-use-nullptr or bugprone-uninitialized-local-variable. A typical configuration lives in a. clang-tidy YAML file at the project root where you list Checks and other options. A common pattern is to enable broad categories with a wildcard and then explicitly disable specific checks you don’t want. For instance, Checks: 'clang-diagnostic-*,modernize-*,readability-*,bugprone-*,-readability-magic-numbers' enables many useful rules but excludes magic-number noise. The compilation database is essential because Clang-Tidy uses the exact compiler flags and include paths from compile_commands. json to parse each file correctly. A frequent misconception is that more checks are always better; on a large legacy codebase, enabling everything creates too many warnings. Instead, start with a curated set, run fixes iteratively, and expand checks as the code stabilizes. Integrate Clang-Tidy into CI and treat new warnings as gating criteria. In practical terms, how checks are named and how to enable or disable them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Clang-Tidy needs to know how each file is compiled. The standard way to supply this information is a compilation database named compile_commands. json. With CMake you enable this by setting CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS to ON, then configuring the project. Practically, create a build directory, run cmake.. from that directory, and CMake will write compile_commands. json into the build tree. A common workflow is: create the source tree with CMakeLists. txt, set the export option, run cmake from a clean build folder, and then run clang-tidy with -p pointing to that build folder. A misconception is expecting compile_commands. json in the source root automatically; it lives in the build directory that CMake produced. Another subtlety: some build systems or wrapper tools move or rewrite paths, so verify the paths in compile_commands. json match your source layout. Key takeaway: always generate the compilation database before running Clang-Tidy so diagnostics reflect actual compiler flags and include paths. Generate compile_commands.json with CMake means it provides per-file compile flags and include paths so static checks parse files accurately.. In practical terms, provide context so clang-tidy analyzes files with real flags and includes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception.
